newsitem.title: USA: Baxter, others may seek triple damages.
newsitem.headline: Baxter, others may seek triple damages.

text.p: Baxter International Inc said Wednesday that it, Becton, Dickinson and Co and Johns Hopkins School of Medicine may seek up to triple damages, plus attorneys fees, after a jury awarded them $2.3 million in a patent infringement case.

On Tuesday, CellPro Inc said it would appeal the $2.3 million jury award against it, stemming from a patent lawsuit over the use of an antibody in bone marrow transplants. A jury in federal district court here found that CellPro willingfully infringed upon patents held by Johns Hopkins and licensed to Becton Dickinson and Baxter.

In a statement, Baxter said it, Johns Hopkins and Becton Dickinson expect to seek injunctive relief from CellPro's sales of its stem cell separation products, which were found to infringe the patents.

Baxter also said it is seeking approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for its Isolex 300 Magnetic Cell Separator System, which uses this technology. The Isolex system also has exclusive status as an orphan device in Japan, and clinical trials for regulatory approval there were completed recently.

Baxter said regulatory filings also are being prepared for Australia and Canada, and are expected to be submitted later this month. Baxter said it also received approvals for product sales in Argentina, Hong Kong, Israel, New Zealand and Singapore.

CellPro said earlier this month it was seeking licenses or other action from the U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services to provide certain patients access to an antibody used in CellPro's CEPRATE SC Stem Cell Concentration System.
CellPro said at the time that the license from the secretary would ensure continued availability of the systems if it should be enjoined from selling the antibody because of the patent litigation.
In its statement, Baxter called CellPro's filing "a ploy to avoid the consequences of their infringement."
